passage:
Tuesday night, hostel.
Zainab talked to me for two hours on the steps behind the library. She hasn't been to lectures in three weeks. She said she lies awake till four and then can't get up, and that her family thinks she's topping the class. "Don't tell anyone, Yusuf. Please."
I'm so torn. She trusted me, and I don't want to be the one who ruins that. But I can't stop thinking about her face when she said, "I'm so tired of everything." I'm angry too, honestly, at how much pressure she's under.
I asked her straight out if she felt safe. She said yes, just exhausted. So I asked her to see the college counsellor, and said I'd walk her there. She said, "Tomorrow, 11." We agreed she'd call me or the warden tonight if it gets worse. At midnight I knocked; she answered and said she was going to sleep. I've set an alarm.

qa.q: How long has Zainab been missing lectures?
qa.a: She hasn't been to lectures in three weeks.

qa.q: What is Yusuf torn between, and what worries Yusuf most?
qa.a: Yusuf is torn between loyalty to Zainab's trust and worry, especially about her saying "I'm so tired of everything", and also feels angry about the pressure on her.

qa.q: Which steps did Yusuf take that were wise?
qa.a: Yusuf asked directly whether she felt safe, agreed she would call Yusuf or the warden that night if things got worse, checked on her at midnight, and offered to walk her to the college counsellor at a set time.

qa.q: What might it mean to Zainab that Yusuf will walk with her?
qa.a: She may feel less alone and more able to face the counsellor, since carrying it by herself had become exhausting.

grounding: A young adult entrusted with Zainab's troubles feels torn between loyalty and worry, and urges Zainab to get qualified help instead of carrying it alone.

passage:
In the college hostel common room, Kishore sat with his head in his hands while the cricket match played on the TV.
"I haven't slept properly in two weeks," he told Harish. "I drink a bit every night just to switch off. My marks are falling. Don't tell anyone, okay? My parents would lose it."
Harish felt the weight of it land on him. Kishore was his closest friend. Telling anyone felt like betrayal. Keeping it felt worse.
"I won't tell your parents," Harish said slowly. "But I'm not okay carrying this alone, and I don't think you should either. The counsellor's office is open till five. Let's go together, right now."
"It's not that bad."
"Then it'll be a short chat."
Kishore laughed weakly. At a quarter to five, they walked across the quad together. Harish waited outside the door for an hour.

qa.q: Until what time was the counsellor's office open?
qa.a: The counsellor's office is open till five.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when Kishore asked him not to tell?
qa.a: Harish felt torn and anxious, caught between loyalty to his closest friend and worry that keeping the secret was worse.

qa.q: What did Harish do that fits a wise response?
qa.a: He urged Kishore to see a qualified counsellor and walked there with him that same afternoon, instead of carrying it alone.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel walking to the counsellor's office?
qa.a: Kishore might feel nervous and a little embarrassed, but also relieved not to face his troubles alone.

grounding: It shows a young adult told about a friend's troubles, torn between loyalty and worry, who takes the friend to a qualified counsellor.

passage:
Dear Elizabeth,
I've been thinking about what you told me on Sunday since the moment you left. I'm writing because I can say it better this way.
You said he checks your phone every night, that he keeps your bank card "to help you save," and that you've stopped seeing your sister because he doesn't like her. You asked me not to tell anyone, and I haven't.
But I'm scared for you. I'm angry at him, too, though that's not the point. This doesn't sound like love that lets you breathe.
I'm not going to go behind your back. But I'm asking you to talk to someone who knows about this, like the women's helpline or a counsellor, and I will sit next to you when you call. Tomorrow, if you want.
If you ever feel unsafe, call me any time, and I will come and get you.
I'm on your side. Always.
Ritu

qa.q: What did Elizabeth say he keeps "to help you save"?
qa.a: He keeps your bank card.

qa.q: What emotions is Ritu feeling as she writes?
qa.a: Ritu feels scared for Elizabeth and angry at him, torn between keeping her promise and her worry.

qa.q: What does Ritu ask Elizabeth to do?
qa.a: Ritu asks Elizabeth to talk to someone qualified, like the women's helpline or a counsellor, and offers to sit beside Elizabeth during the call, tomorrow if Elizabeth wants.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Elizabeth might feel supported and less alone, even if Elizabeth is also scared or unsure about taking the step.

grounding: It shows a young adult holding a friend's worrying confidence, torn between loyalty and worry, urging the friend to contact qualified help instead of carrying it alone.

passage:
The hardest thing I've kept? I'm Rekha, and this was two years ago, in our shared flat.
My flatmate Pooja came home one night and locked herself in the bathroom. When she came out, she told me a senior at her office had been sending her messages at midnight, standing too close in the lift, saying her appraisal "depends on how friendly she is." She begged me not to tell anyone.
I didn't sleep. I was so angry. And scared for her. But I also knew she shouldn't carry this alone, and neither should I.
The next morning I said, "I won't tell anyone behind your back. But your office has a complaints committee for exactly this. I'll help you write it down, and I'll go with you."
We wrote every date and message together. I sat in the corridor while she went in.
The senior was moved to another branch. Pooja still sends me a message every year on that date. Just a heart.

qa.q: Where did Rekha sit while Pooja went in?
qa.a: Rekha sat in the corridor while Pooja went in.

qa.q: How was Rekha feeling the night Pooja told her?
qa.a: Rekha felt angry and scared for Pooja, unable to sleep, torn between Pooja's wish for secrecy and her worry.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that fits a wise response?
qa.a: She didn't go behind Pooja's back but urged her to use the office complaints committee, helped her write everything down, and went with her.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel when she sends a heart every year?
qa.a: Pooja likely feels grateful and bonded to Rekha, remembering that she didn't have to face it alone.

grounding: A young adult recounts being torn over a friend's workplace harassment secret and helping her go to the proper committee instead of carrying it alone.

passage:
Tuesday: In the hostel room, Yamini told Vasudha she hadn't slept properly in weeks and was failing two papers. "Don't tell anyone. Especially not my parents." Vasudha agreed to keep it between them and urged her to see the college counsellor. Yamini said maybe.
Friday night: Near midnight, Yamini said quietly, "Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me." Vasudha's heart pounded. She took Yamini's hand. "I'm staying right here with you. And I can't keep this one to myself. I'm calling the warden now." Yamini cried but didn't stop her. The warden came within ten minutes, sat with them both, and called the college counselling helpline. Someone stayed with Yamini all night.
The following Wednesday: Yamini had seen the counsellor twice. She was still a bit cross with Vasudha. But at dinner she squeezed her hand and said, "Thank you for not carrying it alone." Vasudha realised she had been holding her breath for a week.

qa.q: How soon did the warden come on Friday night?
qa.a: Within ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when Yamini spoke on Friday night?
qa.a: Vasudha's heart pounded; Vasudha felt frightened and torn about the promise, but put Yamini's safety first at once.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do on Friday night that was right?
qa.a: Stayed with Yamini, said plainly this couldn't be kept secret, and called the warden straight away, who brought in the counselling helpline that night.

qa.q: How does Yamini feel about Vasudha by the following Wednesday?
qa.a: Yamini is still a bit cross but grateful, thanking Vasudha for not carrying it alone.

grounding: Shows a young adult torn between loyalty and worry over a friend's troubles, urging help and involving qualified people at once when danger appears.
